clues: A fuzzy, negatively charged coating on the outer surface of eukaryotic plasma membranes.
It is composed of oligosaccharide side chains attached to integral membrane glycoproteins and glycolipids.
It stains positively with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and mediates cell-to-cell recognition and adhesion.
A prominent, spherical, non-membrane-bound basophilic body inside the interphase nucleus.
It forms around chromosomal regions containing tandem repeats of ribosomal genes.
It is the site of rRNA synthesis and assembly of small and large ribosomal subunits.
A network of anastomosing membrane tubules lacking attached ribosomes.
It is richly developed in hepatocytes, skeletal muscle fibers, and steroid-producing endocrine cells.
It carries out lipid and steroid synthesis, cytochrome P450 detoxification, and calcium sequestration.
A juxtanuclear stack of flattened, curved membrane-bound cisternae with distinct cis and trans faces.
It appears as a pale unstained halo (negative image) next to the nucleus in plasma cells.
It modifies, sorts, and packages proteins from the rough ER into secretory vesicles or lysosomes.
A small spherical single-membrane organelle containing oxidative enzymes and often a crystalline nucleoid core.
It performs beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids without generating ATP.
It uses catalase to break down toxic hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
An unusual four-tailed phospholipid found almost exclusively in one specific double-membrane organelle.
It makes up roughly one-fifth of the lipids in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
It restricts proton leakage across cristae to maintain the electrochemical gradient for ATP synthesis.
A large ATPase motor protein arranged as inner and outer arms along peripheral microtubule doublets.
It generates sliding forces between adjacent doublets to bend cilia and flagella.
Genetic deficiency of this protein causes primary ciliary dyskinesia and Kartagener syndrome.
A yellowish-brown granular cytoplasmic inclusion representing indigestible lipid peroxidation remnants.
It is enclosed within residual bodies and is known as the wear-and-tear pigment of aging.
It accumulates prominently in long-lived postmitotic neurons and cardiac muscle cells.
An energy-dependent form of programmed cell death mediated by intracellular caspase proteases.
Affected cells shrink, condense their chromatin, and bud into membrane-bound fragments.
Unlike necrosis, it preserves plasma membrane integrity and does not provoke inflammation.
